That was wrong — 129,049 and 120,098 are BOTH 2022 figures (pre- and post-revision), which is why 120,098 is our canonical 2022 value. 117,746 is the Anuario 2023 total. population_scenarios.headline: Against the official end-2021 stock, the gap by end-2025 is 1.97-2.79 million (17.8-25.1%); the central scenario is 2.53 million (22.8%), leaving about 8.58 million living against 9.43 million officially -- of which 1.68 million is decline ONEI itself published and 0.85 million is this paper's correction. Roughly 92% of the gap is emigration, counting both the 2022-25 flow and the pre-2021 backlog still on the roll.

provisional_schedule_residual_2024_2025.status: provisional — coarse 2019 CDR bridge; refine with full age-sex cells
provisional_schedule_residual_2024_2025.method: Registered minus expected deaths: 2019 total deaths / 2019 population × year-t population (ONEI 3.15 + claims population path).
provisional_schedule_residual_2024_2025.note: Do not call this a Kitagawa decomposition or the primary scientific claim. Primary headcount uncertainty remains the migration scenario envelope.

excess_mortality.note: Always label crude vs schedule residual. Windows differ (2020–2025 vs 2024–2025).
excess_mortality.superseded_note: The crude 2019-CDR bridge charges the entire ageing shift (20.4% -> ~26% aged 60+) to 'crisis'. attributable_mortality replaces it with indirect age standardisation, which lowers the 2024-2025 figure from 77k to ~50k. Keep the provisional numbers only for traceability against earlier versions.

attributable_mortality.method: Indirect age standardisation on {0-14, 15-59, 60-64, 65+}. 2019 rates = ONEI 3.15 deaths / ONEI 3.3 mid-year population. Age structure OBSERVED 2019-2022 (ONEI 3.3 publishes mid-year population by age annually to 2022); 2023-2026 cohort-projected from the observed 2022 structure.

annual_2026_scenario.note: Depends on the +4% registered-death continuation in model_from_2021.py — scenario, not observation.

decomposition_2025.note: Change in annual deaths vs 2019 = size + ageing + rate, exactly per draw. A ~2.0M smaller resident population should have cut ~19,500 deaths a year; ageing added ~22,400; the residual against the 2019 schedule added ~28,500. The two upward terms sum to more than the observed 31,300 rise because the smaller population pulls the other way.

attributable_mortality.headline_en: Excess mortality against the 2019 age-specific schedule runs at roughly 28,500 deaths a year at 2025 levels (prior sensitivity range 18,600-38,200), against ~22,400 a year explained by population ageing alone.
attributable_mortality.headline_es: El exceso respecto de la tabla de 2019 corre a unas 28,500 muertes anuales en exceso a niveles de 2025 (rango de sensibilidad 18,600-38,200), frente a ~22,400 anuales que explica el envejecimiento por si solo.
attributable_mortality.status: primary age-standardised estimate; supersedes the crude 2019-CDR bridge
attributable_mortality.revision_note: 2026-08-03 adversarial review: the previous version derived the elderly count as (share x official total), which made it FALL 67k in 2024 because the official total absorbs ONEI's 2023 register catch-up in one step; and it used 3.12 shares rather than ONEI 3.3 observed age denominators. Both are fixed. 2024-2025 moved 47.1k -> 50.2k and 2022 moved 7.4k -> 12.8k.
caveats: Age structure observed only through 2022 (ONEI 3.3); 2023-2026 is a cohort projection carrying an explicit horizon-growing noise term.
2019 is a crisis-free anchor with no assumed post-2019 improvement; 2017-2019 mean rates are within 1.1% at ages 65+.
Association with the crisis period, not cause-of-death attribution: blackouts, arboviruses, drug shortages and delayed care are not separately identified.
Shares Dfac with Model D, so attributable deaths and the headcount scenario are not independent.

migration_bridge.u0_M_budget_note: U0 and (M-1)R can double-count the same register lag; report ONEI-anchored (M≈1) beside D.

death_register_revisions.note: A 7.5% single-year removal is the empirical anchor for how much slack the register demonstrably has. It sits just below the Model D Dfac cap of 9%, which is why that cap is retained rather than raised.

cause_specific_standardised.standard: WHO World Standard Population 2000-2025, 18 groups to 85+
cause_specific_standardised.year_2023_note: Cuba submitted 2023 deaths to WHO, but ONEI 3.3 population stops at 2022, so 2023 has no observed denominator and is deliberately not standardised.
cause_specific_standardised.crude_over_standardised_note: Any Cuban crude cause-specific rate is roughly DOUBLE its age-standardised value (2.05-2.08 for circulatory and cerebrovascular). Comparing a Cuban crude rate to a regional standardised rate silently smuggles in that factor.

refuted_claims_internal.claim: Cuba's cardiovascular mortality is ~3x the subregional average
refuted_claims_internal.their_comparison: Cuba all-circulatory CRUDE 313.5 vs regional ischaemic-heart 104.9
refuted_claims_internal.error: crude vs standardised, AND a broader cause category vs a narrower one
refuted_claims_internal.verdict: reversed — Cuba is BELOW the regional figure, not 3x above

refuted_claims_internal.claim: Cuba's stroke mortality is 27x the subregional baseline
refuted_claims_internal.error: an age-specific rate compared to an all-ages rate

cause_specific_standardised.caveat_regional_comparators: The regional figures (104.9, 34.1) are quoted from a secondary source and are assumed to be age-standardised, as PAHO usually reports. They are NOT recomputed here. Confirm against a PLISA export before publishing a ratio.
cause_specific_standardised.diagnosis_dependent_causes_note: Standardised diabetes mortality FELL 36% and neoplasms 6% from 2021 to 2022, during documented insulin stockouts and oncology collapse. As with the cancer sentinel, a falling registered rate for a diagnosis-dependent cause is more plausibly under-diagnosis than improvement. Do not read these as good news.

regional_comparators.what_was_tried: Downloaded the WHO Mortality Database raw files and checked whether a like-for-like Latin American comparator could be computed from the same source as Cuba's own rates.
regional_comparators.finding: It cannot. Of the 64 countries with 2021+ deaths AND 2021+ population in the WHO raw files, the only ones in the Americas are French Guiana, Guadeloupe and Martinique. Every Latin American comparator (Mexico, Colombia, Chile, Argentina, Dominican Republic) has population data ending between 1985 and 2007, so no post-2020 standardised rate can be built for them from this source.
regional_comparators.consequence: 104.9 and 34.1 remain UNVERIFIED. Do not publish a ratio against them. Either export precomputed age-standardised rates from PAHO PLISA (which publishes them directly), or state Cuba's ASMR without a regional ratio. Cuba's own side is solid: ischaemic heart 87.2, cerebrovascular 50.4 per 100k, 2022, WHO World Standard.
regional_comparators.do_not_retry: The WHO raw-file route is closed; this was checked, not assumed.

selectivity_splits.finding: Only median_age_stayers (45) is verifiable: ONEI Indicadores 2025 table 6 gives a median age of 45.0 for the whole resident population, which is not the same concept as "stayers" but is the figure the manuscript uses. The 15/77/8 split and median_age_leavers (30) trace to the Albizu-Campos reports plus a circular reference back to this file. They are expert priors, not measurements.
selectivity_splits.action: Reclassified as expert_prior. The 8% figure is load-bearing (it sets elderly emigration in the cohort projection), so a sensitivity is recorded: moving it from 8% to 0-16% shifts 2025 excess mortality by +/-4,845 and the 2022-2025 cumulative by +/-12,025 -- about a quarter and a fifth of the respective prior sensitivity ranges, NOT the +/-1,500 an earlier version of this file claimed. Corrected 2026-08-04.

estimand_rename_2026_08.to: excess deaths relative to the 2019 age-specific schedule
estimand_rename_2026_08.reason: The same formula returns ~61,900 for 2021, which is a pandemic. A residual against a fixed schedule cannot distinguish health-system deterioration from post-acute COVID, coding drift, mortality displacement, health- selective emigration, or denominator error. "Attributable" requires an identified exposure and cause-of-death evidence; neither exists here.

counterfactual_sensitivity_2025.trend_note: Both fitted pre-crisis slopes have 95% CIs containing zero (2006-2019: +0.236%/yr, p=0.066; 2013-2019: +0.678%/yr, p=0.064). The trend is NOT distinguishable from zero on the available series (low power on 7-10 points), so it is not fitted and propagated. The LOW end of the span is a CI bound from Cuba's own data; the HIGH end is an EXTERNAL prior (regional peers), not a bound the Cuban series permits.
counterfactual_sensitivity_2025.note: This span is comparable to the entire Monte Carlo range and is NOT inside it. We do NOT claim a direction: Cuba's own fitted trends put the excess BELOW the flat anchor, while its regional peers' improvement would put it well above. An earlier version of this file asserted the anchor was more likely to understate; that was a stronger claim than the manuscript makes and has been withdrawn.

infant_mortality.infant_deaths_2025_note: 674 = 9.9/1000 x 68,064 births. DERIVED, not observed: ONEI 3.16 stops at 2022. The 2025 IMR of 9.9 is a REPORTED figure (MINSAP/RCM via press) and is NOT in any ONEI table shipped here.
infant_mortality.caution: The rate rose 98% but the deaths rose ~23%, because live births fell 38%. Report both. The 2019 baseline of 5.0 is itself the most-scrutinised statistic in Cuban vital registration; a literature on late-fetal/early- neonatal reclassification (Berdine, Geloso & Powell 2018) means part of any rise may be relaxation of classification practice rather than deterioration. This cuts against treating the sentinel as high-integrity without caveat.
